# How Concepts Get Named: A Psycholinguistics & Language-Learning Survey

> *Framing for this project.* In the `metric_implementer` setup, a **rubric** is a NAME plus a description of a quality construct; an **LLM judge of capability E** executes that rubric to reproduce an **anchor** judgment; the part no finite rubric+executor can reproduce is the **tacit residual**, with asymptote **τ(E) = lim_{L→∞} G_E(L)** (the gap that survives unlimited words) and a fidelity-vs-budget curve **fidelity(L)** that rises toward a ceiling **1 − τ(E)**. The single load-bearing analogy of this survey is: **putting a name on a quality construct IS articulating it.** Everything below is read through that lens: codability ≈ articulability, the efficient-lexicon complexity–accuracy frontier ≈ fidelity(L), naming-granularity ≈ rubric depth, convergence-on-a-name ≈ common-ground/τ(E) formation, and label feedback ≈ "articulation changes the judgment."

---

## Executive summary

Across developmental psycholinguistics, semantic typology, language-evolution modeling, and emergent-communication ML, the question "how do concepts get named?" has five recurring **answers**, and — more useful to us — six recurring **measurement families**.

**The recurring answers.**

1. **Naming is induction under referential uncertainty.** A single ostension underdetermines reference (the *gavagai* problem, Quine 1960); learners collapse the degrees of freedom with biases (mutual exclusivity, shape bias, whole-object), with cross-situational co-occurrence statistics (Yu & Smith 2007), or with a simplicity prior over lexicons (Frank, Goodman & Tenenbaum 2007). The same structure is "infer a metric from few ambiguous exemplars."
2. **Naming is lossy compression under a complexity–accuracy tradeoff.** Lexicons trade representational complexity I(W;M) against communicative accuracy I(W;U) and sit *near an information-bottleneck optimal frontier* (Zaslavsky, Kemp, Regier & Tishby 2018; Kemp, Xu & Regier 2018). This frontier is the cleanest external formalization of fidelity(L).
3. **Naming happens at a privileged granularity that shifts with expertise.** People default to a "basic level" (Rosch et al. 1976); experts downshift to subordinate names (Tanaka & Taylor 1991). The correct granularity selector is category utility / feature-category mutual information, **not** raw predictiveness (Murphy 1982; Corter & Gluck 1992).
4. **Naming is a community convergence process.** Dyads and populations converge on shared names with measurable dynamics — reduction curves, naming-game convergence times, tipping points (Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs 1986; Baronchelli et al. 2006; Centola et al. 2018) — and the *residual disagreement at convergence* is the empirical signature of τ.
5. **Naming is not inert.** Producing a name can degrade (verbal overshadowing; Schooler & Engstler-Schooler 1990) or sharpen and align (label feedback / Mind Melds; Lupyan 2012; Suffill, van Paridon & Lupyan 2024) the underlying judgment.

**The measurement families** (the deliverable). (i) **Codability = name-agreement entropy** H, a per-construct articulability scalar. (ii) **Complexity–accuracy (IB) frontiers** with two distance-to-optimum scalars (ε, gNID) — fidelity(L) made information-theoretic. (iii) **Convergence dynamics** (reduction curves, t_conv, tipping fractions, residual SND) — τ(E)/common-ground formation. (iv) **Granularity probes** (basic-level RT, category utility, expert downshift) — rubric depth conditioned on E. (v) **Mapping-from-sparse-evidence** (cross-situational learning curves, lag-1 contingent accuracy) — few-shot metric induction and its mechanism. (vi) **Naming-reshapes-concept** designs (verbalize-vs-control) — the built-in control for whether a rubric distorts its anchor. The cross-cutting empirical result that most directly underwrites our project is that **codability is executor- and domain-relative, not intrinsic** (odor is near-ineffable in English but as codable as color for Jahai speakers and wine experts; Majid & Burenhult 2014; Majid et al. 2018) — exactly the claim that τ depends on E.

## Section A — Learning the concept→label mapping

### A.1 The induction problem and the constraints that solve it

Quine (1960) frames the floor of every naming measurement: a point-plus-"gavagai"-plus-rabbit is consistent with infinitely many hypotheses (rabbit, undetached parts, rabbit-stage, the color). No behavioral data fixes reference; the question becomes *which biases collapse the degrees of freedom*, and the operational quantity every paradigm manipulates is **referential uncertainty** (number of candidate referents per labeling event, k).

Children deploy a battery of constraints, each measurable as a **disambiguation rate** against 50% chance:

- **Mutual exclusivity (ME)** — given a known + a novel object and a novel label, pick the novel object (Markman & Wachtel 1988). The canonical 2-AFC instrument; DV = proportion choosing the novel referent.
- **Novel-Name–Nameless-Category (N3C)** — map a novel name to the single nameless object in an array; N3C onset coincides with the vocabulary spurt and predicts faster acquisition (Mervis & Bertrand 1994).
- **Shape bias** — extend a novel label to same-shape objects over same-color/texture (Landau, Smith & Jones 1988), measured by a generalization/extension forced choice with novelty-trap controls.

Critically, standard neural nets do **not** exhibit ME by default — they spread probability to seen labels — and it emerges only with specific learning biases or pragmatic/selection competition (Gandhi & Lake 2020; Vong & Lake "Deep daxes" 2021). This is the model-side codability/articulation test (present a novel input + novel-vs-seen labels; DV = P(novel label)), and it shows that the bias which makes naming tractable is not free.

### A.2 Fast mapping vs. cross-situational learning, and the mechanism diagnostic

Carey & Bartlett (1978) coined **fast mapping**: a single incidental exposure ("the chromium tray, not the blue one") creates a partial lexical entry, with full meaning filling in slowly ("extended mapping"); retention tests at delays (immediate / 1 week / month) separate fast-map success from durable encoding. **Cross-situational learning (XSL)** (Yu & Smith 2007; Smith & Yu 2008 in infants) shows words map to referents by aggregating co-occurrence across individually ambiguous trials; the **learning curve** (accuracy vs. number of exposures, with tunable within-trial ambiguity k) is the direct analog of fidelity vs. evidence budget.

The deepest methodological yield is the **mechanism diagnostic**. Aggregate accuracy cannot tell whether learners carry one hypothesis or many. **Trial-contingent / lag-1 conditional accuracy** (Trueswell, Medina, Hafri & Gleitman 2013; "propose but verify") splits accuracy on instance *n* by the outcome of the previous instance of that word. Single-hypothesis predicts ~chance after a wrong prior guess (no residual partial knowledge); associative accounts predict above-chance. Trueswell et al. found the single-hypothesis signature (accuracy after a correct prior ~.46–.49; after an incorrect prior ~.20 = chance with 5 referents), replicated in 2–5-year-olds (Aravind et al. 2018: 78% after success, ~28% = chance after failure). The recall estimator **a = (accuracy − chance)/(1 − chance)** converts the split into a probability-of-retention parameter.

This story is then *matured by three controls* essential before transplant:
- **Decay mimics single hypothesis** (Yurovsky & Frank 2015): a memory-limited multi-hypothesis store whose non-target traces have decayed below detectability produces the same lag-1 signature. A chance-level post-error result indicates *low retained state under load*, not necessarily one-hypothesis storage.
- **Partial knowledge hides below the readout** (Yurovsky, Fricker, Yu & Smith 2014): a savings / re-exposure probe shows "wrong" items relearn faster, so failure ≠ nothing-stored.
- **Test-format inflation** (Smith, Smith & Blythe 2009): a reduced test set lets a non-integrating heuristic beat uniform chance; the correct baseline is the analytic heuristic-learner score under the *exact* test format, not 1/k.

Computational accounts span the storage continuum: associative full-storage with attention biases (Kachergis, Yu & Shiffrin 2012), single-hypothesis Pursuit with retained latent alternatives (Stevens, Yang, Trueswell & Gleitman 2017), and the Bayesian size-prior model P(L) ∝ e^(−α|L|) that makes ME, fast mapping, and social generalization fall out of one inference (Frank, Goodman & Tenenbaum 2007/2009; social cues raised max F from 0.37 to 0.43). The Bayesian model's **precision/recall/F against a gold CHILDES lexicon, swept over α**, is a ready-made supervised complexity–accuracy curve (α = the budget knob).

### A.3 Comprehension read-outs and L2 acquisition

Comprehension is measurable before production via looking-based methods: the Intermodal Preferential Looking Paradigm (Golinkoff et al. 1987; Golinkoff, Ma, Song & Hirsh-Pasek 2013) and Looking-While-Listening (Fernald et al. 1998, 2008), where accuracy = target/(target+distractor) in a 367–2000 ms window and RT = the distractor→target shift latency (which drops ~300 ms between 15–24 months). These are the production-free read-outs of a learned name — analogous to scoring a judge's verdict without requiring it to verbalize.

Second-language vocabulary research gives the population-scale machinery: Nation's nine-component word-knowledge framework (form/meaning/use × receptive/productive) turns "knowing a word" into a multi-cell scorecard (Nation 2001/2013); the **Vocabulary Knowledge Scale** (Wesche & Paribakht 1996) measures graded partial articulation; the **Involvement Load Hypothesis** (Laufer & Hulstijn 2001) makes "cognitive effort" an ordinal budget (need + search + evaluation, each 0/1/2) that predicts retention; **exposure thresholds** (~8–10 reading encounters for reliable multi-aspect uptake; Pellicer-Sánchez & Schmitt 2010) give a budget-vs-uptake curve; and **lexical-coverage thresholds** (95% minimal / 98% adequate; Hu & Nation 2000) give a coverage–accuracy step function. Self-claimed knowledge is corrected for over-claiming via a signal-detection Yes/No-plus-pseudoword design (Meara; Huibregtse, Admiraal & Meara 2002) — a planted-distractor calibration importable to LLM self-reports.

### A.4 Distributional / usage-based acquisition and grounded models

The distributional hypothesis (Harris 1954; Firth 1957) is the bottom-up limit: meaning recoverable from co-occurrence alone — the text-only-executor baseline. **Contextual diversity** (number of distinct documents a word appears in) beats raw frequency as a predictor of both age-of-acquisition and naming RT (Adelman, Brown & Quesada). **Age of Acquisition** itself is a per-word population codability scalar (Kuperman, Stadthagen-Gonzalez & Brysbaert 2012; Wordbank/CDI, Frank et al. 2017), and it has a model-internal analog: Chang & Bergen (2022) define a word's AoA inside an LM as the **sigmoid midpoint of its per-word surprisal-drop trajectory across training checkpoints**, then regress it on the same predictors as children's AoA (finding LMs over-weight frequency, under-weight concreteness). Portelance et al. (2023) show LM surprisal of child-directed speech predicts cross-linguistic child AoA.

Grounded models close the loop. Vong, Wang, Orhan & Lake (2024) train a CLIP-style contrastive model on one child's headcam video+speech (SAYCam-S) and recover word→referent mappings (61.6% top-1 over 22 concepts in 4-AFC, vs. 66.7% for CLIP on 400M web pairs and 26.7% shuffled-cooccurrence chance) — the gold-standard machine analog of the disambiguation test, executor-agnostic. The grounding *debate* bounds the residual: Bender & Koller (2020) argue form-only systems cannot recover communicative meaning (the octopus), Merrill et al. (2021) prove some semantic relations are unrecoverable from form alone (a theorem-grade non-zero residual), while Søgaard (2023) shows ~2/3 of visual concepts retrieve their correct word from text-only embeddings via a linear map (P@100 = 0.68), and the Representational Alignment Hypothesis (2026) finds vision largely *redundant* with text. The empirical convergence: **text-only recovers most but not all of human grounding, and multimodality adds a small increment that behaves like "more text"** (Lancaster sensorimotor benchmark: multimodal > text-only in only 5/7 comparisons; Jones, Trott & Bergen 2024: MLLMs pick up shape/color but not size/orientation/volume) — i.e., 1 − C is small, nonzero, and **construct-typed**.

### A.5 Iconicity bootstrapping

Non-arbitrary form-meaning mapping (iconicity) is the cheapest end of the articulation-cost axis. Iconicity is measurable by a 7-point rating norm at scale (Winter et al. 2024, ~14,000 words) and concentrates in sensory vocabulary (Winter et al. 2017). The Sound-Symbolism Bootstrapping Hypothesis (Imai et al. 2008; Imai & Kita 2014) holds iconicity scaffolds entry into the arbitrary lexicon — but Nielsen & Dingemanse (2021) distinguish strongly-supported *local* enhancement (iconic words themselves easier) from unsupported *general* enhancement, and flag systematicity as a confound. The division-of-labor result (Monaghan, Christiansen & Fitneva 2011) is the cleanest cousin of rubric-granularity tradeoffs: **arbitrariness aids individuation, systematicity aids categorization, iconicity aids communicability** — each form serves a distinct function, predicting a U-shaped optimal-grain. A feature-count→fidelity micro-instrument appears in ideophone work: "cumulative iconicity" (count of 0–4 structural correspondences) predicts guessability (Van Hoey et al. 2023; Dingemanse et al. 2016) — identical in shape to "rubric clauses → reproduced judgment," asymmetry (residual unmeasured iconicity) included.

## Section B — Producing & choosing a name

### B.1 Production mechanics: lemma vs. lexeme, and where naming breaks

Speech-production theory decomposes concept→spoken word into stages: conceptual preparation → **lemma** (meaning+syntax) selection → **lexeme** (morpho-phonological form) → articulation (Levelt, Roelofs & Meyer 1999, WEAVER++). Indefrey & Levelt (2004; Indefrey 2011) fix a per-stage time budget for a ~600 ms naming response (concept ~0–175 ms; lemma selection ~175–250; phonological code ~250–330; syllabification ~330–455; phonetic+articulation ~455–600). Selection is competition-by-Luce-ratio (target activation / Σ competitors), so naming difficulty scales with **competitor density** — and **cumulative semantic interference** gives a clean linear per-item cost: each prior same-category item slows the next by ~+16–30 ms, lag-invariant and durable (Howard et al. 2006), produced even without competitive selection by pure error-driven learning (Oppenheim, Dell & Schwartz 2010). This is the analog of "each added rubric clause in a crowded construct neighborhood carries a marginal cost."

The interactive two-step model (Dell 1986; Dell et al. 1997) supplies a **decomposition-by-error-taxonomy instrument**: score every naming attempt into mutually-exclusive categories (correct / semantic / formal / mixed / unrelated / nonword), then fit a 2-parameter model (s-weight = concept→word access; p-weight = word→form retrieval) whose lesionable weights map onto the two stages and **predict a held-out task** (repetition from naming). The double dissociation — semantic errors localize to anterior/posterior temporal cortex, phonological errors to anterior parietal, with no lesion overlap (Schwartz et al. 2011) — is hard evidence that *where articulation breaks* is a separable, localizable stage. The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon (Brown & McNeill 1966) shows articulability is **graded and partially recoverable**: speakers retrieve first-letter (~57%) and syllable-count (~60%) above chance while the full name fails, and TOT/FOK states carry diagnostic, well-calibrated confidence (a meta-d′ signal; Journal of Cognition 2025).

### B.2 Basic-level granularity and the expert downshift

People spontaneously name at a privileged **basic level** ("chair," not "furniture" or "kitchen-chair"), measured by four converging operations (Rosch et al. 1976): fastest free-naming dominance (1,595 basic-level vs. 14 subordinate first-names), fastest category-verification RT, peak attribute-listing, and peak shape-similarity. The basic level is the natural default rubric grain. **Experts downshift**: dog/bird experts verify and spontaneously name at the subordinate level (retriever, warbler) as fast as novices name at basic level, and list more subordinate features (Tanaka & Taylor 1991; graded version in Johnson & Mervis 1997). This is rubric depth conditioned on executor capability E.

The selector matters and is a guardrail for our pipeline. **Cue validity P(category|feature) is monotone toward superordinates** (Murphy 1982) — a one-sided predictiveness metric *systematically over-abstracts* to vacuously general rubrics. The measure that correctly argmaxes the basic level is **category utility** CU = P(c)·Σ_k[P(f_k|c)² − P(f_k)²], which equals feature-category mutual information up to log-vs-prob, with a 1/K (number-of-categories) overfitting normalizer that makes it non-monotone in depth and yields an interior optimum (Corter & Gluck 1992; Gluck & Corter 1985). The lesson: **the granularity selector should be MI-based, not raw predictiveness, and must carry a complexity counter-term.** This is now testable in models — VLMs default to the basic level (Llama-3.2-Vision 60.2%, Molmo 52.3% of Ecoset images) and show a small but significant expert-prompting downshift via a 2-proportion Z-test (arXiv 2503.12530), while also revealing that expert prompting can *lower* accuracy (a caution for our "add expert detail" instinct).

### B.3 Neology and the lexicalization of new concepts

When does a tacit distinction earn a single named clause vs. stay a paragraph? Word-formation censuses show compounding dominates published neology (~45%), then derivation (~29%), borrowing, abbreviation, blends (Ryskina et al., "From sunblock to softblock"), with two testable success drivers — **supply** (the coinage fills a dense lexical-gap neighborhood) and **demand** (its neighborhood is growing) — operationalized via distributional-neighborhood density and frequency-slope with frequency/length-matched controls; supply found robust, demand weaker. Morphological **productivity** is measured by the hapax fraction P = (#hapax-legomena of a pattern)/(total tokens) (Baayen 1992), i.e., the birth-rate of new named constructs. Neologism *diffusion* requires cross-community **dispersion**, not just frequency, to separate adopted names from fads (Stewart & Eisenstein; Grieve et al.). In expert registers, terminologization proceeds largely by *indirect* metaphor (sense-extension of a common word), now quantifiable at scale: metaphor density ranges 43–86 metaphorical words per 1,000 across disciplines, detected by an MIP/transformer pipeline (F1 = 0.76; Li, Shi & Lei 2025).

### B.4 Single word vs. circumlocution — the budget-L law

There is a quantitative law for when a meaning gets a short form. **Word length tracks in-context informativity (surprisal) better than raw frequency** (Piantadosi, Tily & Gibson 2011), so a form is lengthened in proportion to the bits it must carry — the budget knob. The dual law: **the shortest/most-frequent forms carry the most meanings** (meaning-frequency law, #senses ~ f^0.5; Casas et al. 2019), so compact names are inherently the most polysemous and *offload disambiguation to context* — the formal statement of why a short rubric label under-determines and leans on the executor's tacit background (Piantadosi, Tily & Gibson 2012). The controlled demonstration: Zipf abbreviation emerges **only when both an effort-saving pressure and an anti-ambiguity (accuracy) pressure operate** (Kanwal, Smith, Culbertson & Kirby 2017) — i.e., a distinction merits a compact criterion only when it recurs and mis-scoring it is penalized.

## Section C — Why lexicons name as they do

### C.1 Efficient communication and the Information Bottleneck (= fidelity(L))

The single most-cited formalization. A naming system is a soft encoder q(w|m); its quality is two scalars:
- **Complexity** = I(W;M) bits (how detailed the lexicon is), and
- **Accuracy / informativeness** = I(W;U) (info recovered about meaning, equivalently −E[KL] of listener reconstruction).

The IB objective **F_β = I(W;M) − β·I(W;U)** is swept over β (Blahut-Arimoto / deterministic annealing) to trace the *optimal* complexity–accuracy frontier. Two distance-to-optimum scalars recur: **ε** (efficiency loss, ~0.07–0.21 bits for human color systems) and **gNID** (generalized normalized information distance to the nearest optimal system). Color-naming systems across 110 WCS languages sit near-optimal (ε = 0.18 ± 0.07, gNID = 0.18 ± 0.10, β ≈ 1.03; Zaslavsky, Kemp, Regier & Tishby 2018), and the diachronic test shows systems move *along* the frontier over time while beating rotation and random-drift nulls (Zaslavsky et al. 2022). The framework generalizes to kinship (Kemp & Regier 2012, 566 languages, MDL complexity), number (Xu, Liu & Regier 2020), containers (Xu, Regier & Malt 2016), indefinite pronouns (Denic et al. 2022), and quantifiers (van de Pol et al. 2023, MDL ties complexity to LSTM learnability) — and includes informative *limit cases* where efficiency breaks (recursive numerals fall off the frontier, Denic & Szymanik 2024; the colexification "Goldilocks" inverted-U, Brochhagen & Boleda 2022).

Crucially the same instrument runs on machine executors: communicating neural agents land in the human near-optimal range *only with a discrete channel* (Chaabouni et al. 2021); VQ-VIB reproduces human-aligned lexicons when **complexity is capped, not utility maximized** (Tucker et al. 2022/2025, gNID-to-WCS 0.151); neural iterated-learning needs *both* a simplicity and an informativeness pressure to reach the frontier (Carlsson, Dubhashi & Regier 2024, median ε = 0.07); and LLMs under iterated in-context language learning move toward IB-efficiency — but **only the strongest model recovers the full human complexity range; weaker models collapse to low-complexity (coarse) solutions** (Imel & Zaslavsky / Carstensen-Zaslavsky 2025). That collapse curve is τ(E) vs. E rendered as an experiment. A 2025 optimality *theorem* (kinship case study, arXiv 2511.19120) pins the condition: optimality is achievable iff the listener's decoder equals the Bayesian decoder of the speaker, with a certified residual L = H(U) − C + E[D_KL(q̃_s‖q_l)] ≥ H(U) − C.

The runnable codebase (`nogazs/ib-color-naming`) exposes `complexity()`, `accuracy()`, `d_IB()`, and `fit() → (ε, gNID, β*, matched-optimal-encoder)` on any item×label probability matrix — meaning-space-agnostic once you supply a prior p(m) and a conditional p(u|m).

### C.2 Naming games and convergence on convention (= τ(E)/common-ground formation)

How a population settles a shared name is a measurable dynamical process. The minimal naming game (Steels 1995; Baronchelli et al. 2006) tracks three order parameters — total memory N_w(t), distinct words N_d(t), success rate S(t) — and converges via a sharp disorder→order transition with scaling **t_conv ~ N^1.5 mean-field, ~N^1.4 on complex networks**. Humans reproduce this: ~100-person populations spontaneously converge globally under random mixing but settle into competing local conventions on spatial networks (Centola & Baronchelli 2015), and a **committed minority above ~25% flips an established convention** (Centola, Becker, Brackbill & Baronchelli 2018; threshold is parameter-dependent, dropping to <1% under group interactions, Iacopini et al. 2022). The instrument now runs on LLM populations, where conventions emerge spontaneously, **collective bias appears that no individual agent holds**, and per-model tipping thresholds range 2–67% (Ashery, Aiello & Baronchelli 2025) — with the essential leakage caveat that apparent emergence can be memorized convention (Barrie & Törnberg 2025).

At the dyadic scale, **conceptual-pact reduction** is the paragraph→name compression we care about: referring expressions for tangrams drop from 41 to 8 words over 6 rounds while accuracy holds (Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs 1986; words contract to 1–2 in 3–6 reps). The pact is **partner-specific**: term reuse is 48% with the same partner but only 18% with a swapped partner (Brennan & Clark 1996) — the cleanest executor-dependence number, and a direct measure of how much of a name is shared vs. tacit. Hawkins et al. (2020) show reduction is feedback-gated and *differential by part-of-speech* (function words drop 91–94%, nouns only 59%) — a "name kernel" survives, driven by discriminativeness. The CHAI hierarchical-Bayesian model (Hawkins et al. 2023) formalizes the gap between partner-specific idiolect φ_k and the transferable community convention Θ — **the partner-specific residual IS τ(E)** — and ad-hoc conventions generalize to new referents with a Shepard-law similarity decay (Ji et al. 2025). Iterated-learning experiments give a compositionality scalar (topographic similarity / Mantel-z between meaning- and signal-distances; Kirby et al. 2008, 2015) and show structure emerges only under joint compressibility + expressivity pressure.

### C.3 Vagueness, polysemy, and reuse — the within-name residual

Even a perfectly-converged name leaves residual variance, and this floor is measurable. Membership is graded (Rosch 1975; Hampton 2007 dissociates unbounded typicality T from asymptotic membership M, and shows within-person test-retest inconsistency < between-person disagreement — the residual is *structured*, not noise). Four instruments quantify the within-name floor: **goodness-of-example ratings + verification RT** (the typicality battery); **hedge-acceptability** ("sort of X"; Lakoff 1973); **borderline-contradiction acceptance** forming an inverted-U peaking at the borderline (44.7% accept "tall and not tall" at the median; Alxatib & Pelletier 2011); and the **RSA threshold-posterior** whose spread is quantified residual vagueness (Lassiter & Goodman 2017). Order effects localize the residual to the *naming* step specifically (present in linguistic categorization, absent in pure perceptual matching; Égré, de Gardelle & Ripley 2013). A mixture-IRT model decomposes total disagreement into **criterial vagueness** (which criterion a rater uses — the articulable part) vs. **degree vagueness** (where the threshold sits within a fixed criterion — the residual) (Verheyen, Egré et al. 2019) — the single most directly portable separation of articulable from tacit. Functional ambiguity is *adaptive*: efficient codes reuse cheap forms because context disambiguates (Piantadosi, Tily & Gibson 2012), and colexification follows the Goldilocks inverted-U (relatedness raises shared naming up to a confusability ceiling; Brochhagen & Boleda 2022; Karjus et al. 2021's causal experiment shows similarity drives merging *only until* need-to-distinguish overrides it).

## Section D — The limits & effects of naming

### D.1 Codability and ineffability across domains (= articulability, executor-relative)

**Codability** — how reliably/compactly a referent can be named — is the 70-year-old psycholinguistic ancestor of articulability (Brown & Lenneberg 1954), operationalized as a triad: **name-agreement entropy H, naming latency (RT), and name length**, with high codability predicting recognition memory. The canonical scalar is **H = −Σ_i p_i log₂ p_i** over the distinct names a population gives one referent (Snodgrass & Vanderwart 1980); H = 0 is perfect consensus. H **predicts naming RT better than %-modal-agreement** — the keystone validation being van Hoef, Lynott & Connell (2024): across 800 photos, H alone explains adj R² = .423 of RT (~185 ms per H-unit, up to 678 ms), while a modal-name model explains only .088, and a *full-distribution-weighted* model beats the modal-only model by BF₁₀ = 1442.50. The mandate for our pipeline is direct: **use soft agreement over the whole label distribution, not modal-name match.** LinguaPix (Krautz & Keuleers 2022) supplies the sample-size-corrected normalized entropy H/log(n) and large open calibration corpora.

The cornerstone result for τ(E): **codability is a property of (domain × namer), not intrinsic.** Odor is near-ineffable in English (5× longer, source-based "smells-like-X" descriptions) but as codable as color for Jahai speakers, who use dedicated abstract terms (Majid & Burenhult 2014; language × domain interaction F(1,90) = 88.47). Across 20 languages there is no universal sense hierarchy and the domain × language interaction dominates (χ² ≈ 700; Majid et al. 2018 PNAS, using Simpson's diversity validated against Shannon H at r = −0.97 and Brown-Lenneberg agreement at r = 0.95). Expertise raises codability *narrowly and non-transferably*: wine experts are more consistent only for wine and only in their domain; coffee experts gain nothing for coffee (Croijmans & Majid 2016), and the expert's perceptual skill is *dissociable* from naming — verbal interference does not impair experts' wine-odor recognition (Croijmans et al. 2021), establishing that "can name it" and "can judge it" are separable executor capacities. The connectivity account (Olofsson & Gottfried 2015) supplies a τ(E) *floor*: some tacitness is a universal neurocognitive bottleneck no lexicon erases. Net honest position: 1 − C is small, nonzero, construct-dependent, and executor-relative.

Other off-the-shelf nameability predictors: Shape Naming Divergence (SND = mean proportion of words in a free description appearing in no other description; Zettersten & Lupyan 2020), with low SND causally improving category learning; and concreteness/abstractness norms (Brysbaert et al. 2014, 40k words) as a feature to predict articulability before running an executor.

### D.2 Does naming change the concept? — label feedback and linguistic relativity

Naming is two-directionally non-inert.

**Distortion (verbal overshadowing).** Verbalizing a face/wine/color *degrades* later non-verbal recognition (Schooler & Engstler-Schooler 1990). The honest size is small and timing-moderated: meta-analytic Fisher Z_r = −0.12 (~12%; Meissner & Brigham 2001); the 33-lab Registered Replication found ~4% (immediate) to ~16% (delayed) (Alogna et al. 2014). Crucially the effect concentrates exactly where perceptual skill outstrips verbal skill — the *taste residual* case (Melcher & Schooler 1996: only intermediate wine drinkers, not novices or experts, are hurt). This is the direct warning that forcing a rubric where the signal is tacit can lower fidelity.

**Sharpening / alignment (label feedback).** The mirror image: hearing/producing a label sharpens categorical perception, lifts detection d′ (Lupyan 2012; Lupyan & Ward 2013, effects decay >~1600 ms = transient feedback), and **raises inter-rater alignment** even with redundant arbitrary labels, fully mediated by increased categoricality (Suffill, van Paridon & Lupyan 2024, "Mind Melds"; alignment .20 vs .12 with vs without labels). Linguistic relativity supplies the boundary case: a lexical category boundary speeds cross-boundary discrimination (Russian *siniy/goluboy*: 173 ms vs. 14 ms cross-category advantage; Winawer et al. 2007), an effect abolished by verbal but not spatial interference and lateralized to the language hemisphere (Gilbert et al. 2006) — i.e., the boundary effect rides on the *name*.

Both directions are governed by the same knob: a label helps when name↔target match is strong and hurts when discrepant (Lupyan & Swingley 2012). The **verbalize-vs-control between-subjects design is the built-in control** for whether adding a written rubric moves a judge's verdict relative to no-rubric.

---

## Consolidated measurement-methods table

| Method | Subfield | What it measures | How | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Name-agreement entropy H | Codability norms | Per-construct codability/articulability | H = −Σ p_i log₂ p_i over free names; regress RT on H | Sensitive to synonym canonicalization; population-relative |
| Disambiguation-rate FC (ME/N3C) | Dev. word learning | Strength of bias fixing a 1-trial mapping | Familiar+novel object, novel label; DV vs 50% | Forced choice can manufacture above-chance; binary |
| Cross-situational learning curve | XSL | Acquisition rate under ambiguity k | k words×k pics/trial; AFC test; accuracy vs exposures | Test-format inflation; aggregate hides mechanism |
| Lag-1 contingent accuracy | XSL mechanism | Single- vs multi-hypothesis state | Split acc(n) by outcome of prior instance; a=(acc−ch)/(1−ch) | Decay mimics single-hypothesis; needs many items |
| Communication accuracy (name→reconstruct) | Codability/reference | Functional codability on held-out decoder | Encoder names; separate decoder picks referent; %correct | Confounds encoder skill with construct codability |
| IB complexity–accuracy frontier (ε, gNID) | Efficient comm. | fidelity(L) + distance to optimum | I(W;M) vs I(W;U); sweep β; ε, gNID via fit() | Needs meaning space + prior; MI biased on small matrices |
| Simplicity–informativeness Pareto vs random | Semantic typology | Efficiency vs hypothetical systems | MDL complexity vs expected KL cost; Monte-Carlo null | Frontier depends on hypothesis space + need dist. |
| Basic-level / verification RT + downshift | Categorization | Default naming grain, expert shift | Free naming + RT by level; experts vs novices | RT effects small; "basic level" culture-dependent |
| Category utility (argmax granularity) | Categorization | Optimal naming level | CU = P(c)Σ[P(f|c)²−P(f)²], 1/K normalizer | Needs feature norms; cue validity fails (over-abstracts) |
| Naming-game order params + t_conv | Lang. evolution | Convergence to shared name | Track N_w, N_d, S; t_conv ~ N^1.5 | Abstract agents; convergence often guaranteed |
| Committed-minority tipping point | Social convention | Convention brittleness/revisability | Inject minority fraction; find flip threshold (~25%) | Threshold parameter-dependent (memory, group size) |
| Conceptual-pact reduction + partner swap | Reference games | Compression + partner-specific residual | Words/ref over rounds; reuse same vs new partner (48%→18%) | Free-text coding; practice-effect confound |
| Verbalize-vs-control (overshadowing) | Memory/relativity | Whether naming distorts judgment | Describe vs filler, then recognition; accuracy Δ | Small (Z_r=−0.12), fragile, timing-moderated |
| Mind-Melds alignment | Label feedback | Whether naming raises inter-rater alignment | Sort w/ vs w/o redundant label; alignment via RSA | Alignment can rise without validity (herding) |
| Mixture-IRT vagueness decomposition | Vagueness | Criterial vs degree (residual) vagueness | 2-group IRT on test-retest categorization | Assumes few latent criterion-groups |
| RSA threshold-posterior spread | Vagueness/RSA | Quantified residual vagueness | Fit posterior over threshold θ; spread = residual | Assumes single ordered dimension |
| Gold-lexicon P/R/F + AFC top-k | Comp. word learning | Mapping quality vs ground truth | Compare inferred to gold lexicon; sweep prior | Gold lexicon ill-defined; F conflates error types |
| Model-internal AoA (surprisal sigmoid) | Comp. acquisition | When a construct becomes learnable by E | Per-word surprisal across checkpoints; sigmoid midpoint | Surprisal ≠ production; threshold-fit choices |
| Picture-naming RT regression | Production | Naming difficulty + its predictors | Voice-onset RT ~ H + AoA + freq + complexity | Confounded by frequency/length; production-only |
| Cumulative semantic interference slope | Production | Marginal per-competitor naming cost | RT ~ ordinal position within category (~+16–30 ms/item) | Mechanism (concept vs lexical) debated |

---

## Cross-field synthesis: a taxonomy of naming-measurement strategies

The methods above sort into six strategies, each answering a different sub-question of "how nameable is this, and what does naming it do?"

1. **Codability / name-entropy** (Brown & Lenneberg 1954; Snodgrass & Vanderwart 1980; Majid et al. 2018; Zettersten & Lupyan 2020). A *per-construct* scalar for "how reliably/compactly is this named." Variants — Shannon H, Simpson's diversity, SND, normalized H/log(n) — are interchangeable up to normalization. Validated against an external cost (naming RT). **Best for**: a cheap articulability score that needs no anchor labels, just a panel of namers.

2. **Complexity–accuracy efficiency curves** (Zaslavsky et al. 2018; Kemp, Xu & Regier 2018; Chaabouni 2021; Tucker 2022; Carlsson 2024; Imel & Zaslavsky 2025). A *system-level* frontier with an optimal envelope and two distance-to-optimum scalars (ε, gNID). **Best for**: fidelity(L) made information-theoretic, with an "is this rubric on the efficient frontier?" diagnostic and an executor-capability axis.

3. **Convergence dynamics** (Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs 1986; Brennan & Clark 1996; Baronchelli 2006; Centola 2018; Hawkins 2020/2023; Ashery 2025). *Time-resolved* measures of how a community settles a name, and the *residual at convergence*. **Best for**: τ(E)/common-ground formation, convention brittleness, and the partner-specific (= executor-specific) residual.

4. **Granularity** (Rosch 1976; Murphy 1982; Corter & Gluck 1992; Tanaka & Taylor 1991; arXiv 2503.12530). The *level* at which naming happens and how it tracks expertise, with a validated MI-based selector. **Best for**: rubric depth conditioned on E, with a guardrail against over-abstraction.

5. **Mapping-from-sparse-evidence** (Yu & Smith 2007; Trueswell 2013; Frank, Goodman & Tenenbaum 2007; Yurovsky & Frank 2015). *Learning curves + mechanism diagnostics* for inferring a label from few ambiguous exemplars. **Best for**: few-shot metric induction and whether iterative refinement carries one interpretation or many.

6. **Naming-reshapes-concept** (Schooler 1990; Lupyan 2012; Suffill 2024; Winawer 2007). *Causal* tests of whether the act of naming distorts or sharpens the judgment. **Best for**: the built-in label-feedback control on the rubric-as-anchor loop.

Two cross-cutting cautions that every strategy inherits: **reliability ≠ validity** (high name-agreement / low gNID measures consensus, not correctness — a panel can converge on a wrong or biased name), and **codability is executor-relative** (no executor-free number; the ceiling depends on E's capability, expertise, and background, exactly as τ(E) depends on E).

---

## Connections to articulability (the `metric_implementer` setup)

**Name-entropy / codability as the articulability metric (Column-1 reliability instrument).** For a fixed construct, run an ensemble of judges (or one judge over paraphrase/seed/temperature draws, and/or human annotators) and have each *freely name* the quality that distinguishes high from low exemplars; canonicalize names with the existing leaf re-clustering recipe (embedding + LLM dedup); compute articulability A = 1 − H/log₂(n) over the clustered labels. Low A flags a construct headed for a low fidelity ceiling *before* any expensive scoring. Validate it the Brown-Lenneberg way — regress judge fidelity-to-anchor on A — so it is evidence, not circular (van Hoef 2024 shows H beats modal-match; adopt **soft, whole-distribution agreement**, never top-1). This is a drop-in addition to the scorecard's reliability ρ column and pairs naturally with the existing reconstruction-validity (metric-rediscovery) measure.

**The IB complexity–accuracy frontier as fidelity(L), with ε and gNID.** Treat the rubric+judge as encoder q(label|item): complexity = instruction budget L (tokens/clauses, or I(item; rubric-verdict) in bits); accuracy = I(rubric-verdict; anchor). Build the frontier with the `nogazs/ib-color-naming` `fit()` machinery (or an empirical Pareto envelope over rubric variants), then report **fidelity(L)** = accuracy vs L, with its asymptote = the dense/anchor ceiling 1 − τ(E), **ε** = bits below the best-achievable rubric at this budget (verbose-but-uninformative waste, distinct from the tacit residual), and **gNID** = whether the rubric carves items at the *right granularity*, not just the right amount. This is the principled twin of the project's Kaplan-Meier "fraction articulable at budget B" framing — gNID and ε give the headline distance-to-optimum scalars the frontier currently lacks. Mandatory guardrail: the **rotation/permutation control** (shuffle criterion-to-construct assignments; the real rubric must beat >~90% of variants) before claiming a construct is articulable — this is exactly the §6.5 selection-inflation defense applied at the instrument level (and answers the Gibson "too-permissive frontier" critique).

**Naming-game convergence as τ(E)/common-ground formation.** Run a name-game over a panel of judge agents (optionally heterogeneous E): seed candidate names for a construct, run pairwise reference rounds where matched labels are rewarded and pruned (Baronchelli rule), and track convergence — fraction reaching one low-entropy label, t_conv, and final name-agreement entropy. Constructs that converge fast to low H are highly articulable; constructs that stall in a competing-label oligopoly (the Centola-Baronchelli random-network 33% regime) mark high tacit residual. The **partner-swap rebound** (Brennan & Clark 48%→18%) ports directly: build the minimal rubric on judge A, deploy on judge B, measure the fidelity drop — the non-transferring part is the executor-bound tacit content = τ(E) made concrete. Sweep E across model tiers to test the Imel-Zaslavsky prediction that only strong judges climb the full frontier (the capability at which fidelity stops rising = empirical τ(E)). Mandatory leakage control (Barrie & Törnberg): re-run with token-nulled labels and require convergence to exceed any single judge's isolated agreement.

**Basic-level granularity as rubric depth.** Measure at what level a judge spontaneously names a quality (superordinate axis / basic dimension / subordinate clause) without the rubric, and whether an expert-persona prefix downshifts it (2-proportion Z-test, per arXiv 2503.12530). Select rubric depth with **category utility / feature-category MI**, never raw predictiveness — Murphy's monotonicity theorem says a one-sided fidelity metric will over-abstract to vacuous rubrics, so the 1/K (description-length) counter-term is what produces the interior optimal L and the predicted U-shape. The expert downshift gives a falsifiable claim: optimal rubric specificity should *rise with judge capability E*, directly feeding the scaling-law axis "model tier."

**Mutual-exclusivity / cross-situational learning as inferring a metric from few-shot exemplars.** Iterative rubric refinement *is* XSL: the executor re-encounters a construct across rounds and must commit to an interpretation. Apply the **lag-1 contingent-accuracy diagnostic** — split round-n fidelity by the outcome of round n−1 for that construct, compute the retention coefficient a = (acc − chance)/(1 − chance) — to learn whether refinement carries one interpretation forward (propose-but-verify) or accumulates several (associative). Use the **Same/Switch probe** to detect latent facets the rubric under-articulates (above-chance Switch = stored tacit structure), and the **savings probe** on currently-failed constructs to catch sub-threshold partial articulability. Apply all three with the **Smith-2009 format-honest baseline** (beat the analytic heuristic-learner score — a length/sentiment/position shortcut — not 1/k), which is the same anti-Goodhart discipline the optimizer already uses (fresh CF batches, cross-family holdout).

**Label feedback as "articulation changes the judgment."** The verbalize-vs-control design is the built-in control for the rubric-as-anchor loop: compare the judge's verdict *with* a written rubric vs. a holistic no-rubric verdict. Verbal overshadowing (Schooler 1990; Z_r = −0.12, larger for hard-to-name/tacit constructs and intermediate-skill executors, per Melcher & Schooler) warns that forcing a rubric can *lower* fidelity exactly where the signal is tacit — bounding when pushing L upward backfires. The Mind-Melds direction (Suffill 2024) is the upside: a shared rubric name can *raise* inter-judge alignment, but watch that rising alignment can be herding to the rubric's framing rather than rising validity (always pair alignment Δ with accuracy-vs-anchor). Practically: collect the anchor *before/independently* of naming so the overshadowing/feedback effect is measured, not silently baked in.

---

## Open questions & under-measured areas

- **Abstract-construct meaning spaces.** Every clean IB instrument (frontier, ε, gNID) was built for perceptual domains (color, kinship, container shape) with a defined meaning prior and similarity kernel. Quality constructs ("rigor," "narrative tension," "comment-responsiveness") have no canonical metric space; defining U and the need-prior is the load-bearing modeling step and materially moves ε / I_MU. The frontier should be treated as *comparative* (rubric A vs B vs budget L), not absolute.
- **Codability ≠ validity, formally.** Name-agreement entropy measures intersubjective consensus, which is reliability; it can be high for a wrong/biased name. The field lacks a clean joint instrument that scores codability *and* anchor-validity simultaneously without circularity (the NOVA discriminating-triplet design is a partial answer).
- **The two-layer split (criterial vs degree vagueness) at LLM scale.** Verheyen-Egré mixture-IRT cleanly separates articulable (which criterion) from residual (where the threshold sits), but assumes a small fixed number of latent criterion-groups and many items per criterion — its scaling to LLM-judge panels and the choice of operationalization budget (which determines whether residual leaks into the criterial term) are unmeasured.
- **Does the lag-1 mechanism transfer to LLMs?** "Decay mimics single hypothesis" (Yurovsky & Frank 2015) reinterprets the LLM analog as context dilution / recency bias, not biological forgetting; whether the contingent-accuracy signature is stable across context lengths for a judge is an open empirical question.
- **Self- vs observer-articulability.** Nisbett & Wilson (1977) and the introspection-gap literature predict observer-articulability ≥ self-articulability; the seed-to-frontier gap (community seed rubrics vs the GEPA frontier at fixed L, tier) is a free readout the project flags but the human literature has not quantified for evaluative constructs.
- **Verbal overshadowing for abstract evaluation.** All effect sizes are for perceptual stimuli (faces, wine, color); the magnitude and even sign of "naming changes the judgment" for abstract LLM-judged constructs is unmeasured, and the effect is itself replication-fragile — so it should be tested per-task, not assumed.
- **Convergence vs correctness.** Naming games reward arbitrary coordination; collective bias can manufacture agreement absent in any individual judge (Ashery 2025). Whether a converged rubric tracks the *true* construct (not just a shared label) requires a grounding/fidelity referee in the loop — the same "evaluate, never gate" invariant the project already enforces — and is not addressed by convergence statistics alone.
- **MI estimation on small matrices.** ε and gNID use raw plug-in MI, biased upward when labels are many relative to items (Vinh, Epps & Bailey 2010); chance-corrected variants (AMI / adjusted-NID) and permutation nulls are needed before any rubric-IB claim, and are currently absent from the source codebase.
